## Overexploitation of global fisheries

We will examine the state of global fisheries and seek to reproduce one of the most widely cited examples of species collapse in order to examine the evidence behind an influential paper on global fisheries, [Worm et al. 2006](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1132294). However, rather than using the 1950-2003 dataset available to Worm and colleagues in 2006, we will be drawing from more recent stock assessment data to see how the trends have fared, specifically in Atlantic cod.

We also explore how to understand and manipulate tabular data using relational database concepts. Instead of working with a single independent dataframe, as in Module 1, we will be working with a large relational database consisting of tables of different dimensions, but are related through one or more IDs.

## The Database

We will use data from the [RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database](https://www.ramlegacy.org/database/). Note that the database files are available through Zenodo; please download and unzip the file, moving the .RData file only into your own `data/` folder within this project.

Use the code below to load up the tables in this database.

```{r}
load("data/DBdata[asmt][v4.66].RData")
```

The above function loads all 60 tables of this database, which is a lot! So step one of the data science process is exploring the structure of the database and figuring out how the tables are related.

A selected set of documentation have been provided in `documentation/`. Open up the Database Quickstart Guide for reference as you work through the problems below.

Each row in the stock table includes a identifier for the stock that includes some information about the country the stock resides in, the taxonomic serial number for which kind of fish is present, both the scientific and common names, an area id including the country the stock is in as well as the stock's position inside that country, a more detailed identifier of which country and region the stock belong to, a unique stock id, another area id, and a indicator of whether or not a stock is current / deprecated.

### Q4 (1 point)

There are two main data tables described in section C, but their key attributes are difficult to understand. Join the two main data tables with their respective metrics tables (section D):


```{r}

# bioparams not opening for some reason; assuming same thing that happened with assessment

bioparams[] = lapply(bioparams, function(x) { 
  if (is.character(x)) iconv(x, 
                             from = "latin1",
                             to = "UTF-8") else x })


#view(bioparams)
#view(biometrics)

#using biounique as the key for biometrics --> maps to bioid


bio_params_metrics = bioparams |> 
  left_join(biometrics, join_by(bioid == biounique))



#view(timeseries)
#view(tsmetrics)

#using tsunique as key for tsmetrics --> maps to tsid

ts_params_metrics = timeseries |> 
  left_join(tsmetrics, join_by(tsid == tsunique))

```


-   Briefly describe the contents of each joined table.

-   What is accomplished by joining these tables?

Bioparams table contains IDs for stocks that include their common names and general locations. Each row contains a different biometric being recorded ( bioid ). By joining with biometrics, the table now includes longer descriptions and more detailed categories for the biometric codes used in the bioparams table and indicates what units they are being measured it.  

Timeseries table contains different metrics for a given fish stock and location, each across several years, hence why the table is 1.6 million observations long. By joining with tsmetrics, the joined table now indicates the method used to calculate each metric, a longer description of the metric, and the units each metric is reported in. 




## Overexploitation of Atlantic cod

This database is clearly complex and contains a lot of information. We've grappled with its high dimensionality by exploring and joining tables above. Next, we will take a "bottom-up" approach and evaluate a single species, Atlantic cod. Read this [book chapter](https://pressbooks.pub/extinctionstories/chapter/atlantic-cod/) on Atlantic cod, which serves as a reference for the following questions.

### Q5 (1 point)

The collapse of the Atlantic cod fisheries is well documented. Let's see if we can visualize that decline with this database. 

-   How many unique fish stocks comprise "Atlantic cod" and what regions do they come from?

```{r}

atl_cod_stock = stock |>
  filter(commonname == "Atlantic cod") |>
  group_by(stockid) |>
  unique()

```

There are 28 unique atlantic cod stocks originating in the North American ( Canada, New England, Greenland ) and Northern European ( Iceland, UK, Denmark, Poland, France ) waters of the Northern Atlantic Ocean and North Sea.  


Create a vector of the 'stockid' associated with "Atlantic cod". Then turn your attention to the previously-joined timeseries/tsmetrics table and create a subsetted dataframe with only observations of "Atlantic cod" that have a non-NA value. This table reports many years and many metrics, while we are primarily interested in the years since 1950.

```{r}


stockid_vector = atl_cod_stock |> select(stockid) 

atl_cod_ts_data = ts_params_metrics |> 
  semi_join(stockid_vector, join_by(stockid))


#most_common_ts_stuff = atl_cod_ts_data |> 
 # group_by(tsid) |> 
 # mutate(ts_category_most_common = n()) |> 
  #select(tsid, ts_category_most_common, tscategory) |>
 # unique()



#atl_cod_ts_for_real |> filter(tsshort =="F") |> view()


```



-   Which 2 metrics are most commonly reported for Atlantic cod in this timeframe and what do they mean?

Fishing Mortality and Catch or Landing are the most common metrics. 

Fishing mortality refers to the rate at which fish are removed from a stock by fishing.

Catch refers to the total mass of fish caught on a given trip; landings refers to the percent of the total catch that is brought back with the boat to land. 

In reference to the following question, the most common submetric of Catch or Landings is CdvimeanC-ratio, which compares a given catch of fish to the mean, thereby indicating how many times larger or smaller this individual catch is compared to the long term average. F-1/y is the most common metric to represent Fishing Mortality, and is measured by a value zero or greater that indicates the percentage of a given stock's population removed by fishing in a given year. This percentage is calculated using the formula P = 1 - e^-F, where F is the fishing mortality value. As such, as F increases linearly, the percentage of fish removed approaches 100%. 


### Q6 (1 point)

Make a timeseries figure for each stock of Atlantic cod in a single figure. Rather than coloring by the identity of the stock, color by the region it comes from (this may require joining). Use `facet_*()` to plot the top two metrics from Q5 in a single code chunk. Connect the points for each stock and focus on the period since 1950. Update until the figure is easily interpretable.


```{r}

atl_cod_stock_fusion = atl_cod_stock |>
  select(stockid, region)


atl_cod_ts_for_real = atl_cod_ts_data |>
  left_join(atl_cod_stock_fusion, join_by(stockid))

# getting fishing mortality into a more easily read format

atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue = if_else(atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsid == "F-1/yr", 
                                      true = -expm1(-atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue), 
                                      false = atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue)


#atl_cod_ts_for_real |> filter(assessid == "AFWG-CODNEAR-1943-2021-ICESIMP2024", tsid == "F-1/yr") |> view()
#atl_cod_ts_for_real |> filter(tsid == "F-1/yr") |> arrange(desc(tsvalue)) |> view()



atl_cod_ts_for_real |> 
  filter(as.numeric(tsyear) > 1950, 
         !is.na(tsvalue) == TRUE,
         tscategory == "FISHING MORTALITY" |
           tscategory == "CATCH or LANDINGS",
         tsid == "F-1/yr"| 
           tsid == "CdivMEANC-ratio")|>
  ggplot(aes(x = tsyear, 
             y = tsvalue, 
             color = region,
             group = stockid)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+
  facet_wrap(~tscategory+region, 
             scales = "free_y")+
  labs(color = "Location of Stock", x = "Year", y = "Fraction")




```

-   What happened to Atlantic cod stocks during the period 1950-present? What information does each metric convey?


For Catch or Landings plots, for most stocks in all regions the highest CoL occured in the 1990s up to 2000, when there was a brief pause, and for some stocks more recently the CoL has shot up sharply and subsequently fallen back down slightly. At times when CoL is high, this means the number of fish being caught is greater than the average number of fish caught by the factor listed on the y-axis; this can be interpreted as a measure of expansion of the industry or higher fishing activity during a given time.

For Fishing mortality, percentages started much lower in the 1950s and 60s, and more recently, though there is some fluctuation, the percentages are much higher than they were.
This is a measure of the percent ( multiply y-axis by 10 ) of the fish population removed from a given stock in a given year. So although Catch or Landings was much higher 70 years ago, the high recent fishing mortality indicates modern fish populations are being stretched thinner now compared to previously


There are the most entries for the metric "TCbest-MT" which corresponds to total catch in units of metric tons, so this is what I will focus on for this graph.


"NA" entries are a real problem, so I will replace all of them with zero to facilitate calculation.

```{r}

atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue = if_else(is.na(atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue) == TRUE & 
                                        atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsid == "TCbest-MT", 
                                      true = 0, false = atl_cod_ts_for_real$tsvalue )


atl_cod_ts_plus_extra = atl_cod_ts_for_real |>

         tsyear, 
         tsvalue,

             y = total_regional_catch,
             color = region))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  theme_classic()+
  labs(x = "Year of Measurement",
       y = "Total Cod Catch Across All Regional Stocks ( Metric Tons )",
       color = "Region")

#US contribution is small relative to the others. Faceting around region will allow trends to be identified more easily

atl_cod_ts_plus_extra |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tsyear, 
             y = total_regional_catch,
             color = region))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  theme_classic()+
  labs(x = "Year of Measurement",
       y = "Total Cod Catch Across All Regional Stocks ( Metric Tons )",
       color = "Region")+
  facet_wrap(~region, scales = "free_y")

```

```{r}
important_names = c("1976 MSFCMA", "1996 SFA", "2006 MSFCMRA")


legislation_dates = data.frame(important_dates, important_names)

             y = total_regional_catch,

             aes(xintercept = important_dates,

       color = "Region",

  facet_wrap(~region, scales = "free_y")



```



### Q9 (2 points)

What happened to Atlantic cod stocks for each region following each piece of legislation or management plan, and why do you think this was so? Your multi-paragraph answer should be informed by content from the book chapter and your figure from Q8; additional sources are optional, and all sources should be cited.




In the late 1960s, the Canadian Cod industry reached its global peak production of roughly 5 million metric tons of fish that year. However, in the 7 following years production would decrease by nearly a factor of 5 ( Figure from Q8 ). In 1976, the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (MSFCMA) was passed in the US in an attempt to protect the cod stocks from further depletion. Importantly, the act "protected U.S. waters from foreign fishing vessels", but presumably did not restrict access to US-based fishermen (https://pressbooks.pub/extinctionstories/chapter/atlantic-cod/). As a result, Post-MSFCMA US cod production actually increased significantly while Canada's dropped further. Then, Canadian production seemed to increase by almost 30%, which was most likely because the cod populations had time to respawn in the American stocks that were only exploited about 1/10th as much as those in Canada ( Figure from Q8 ); this level of production was sustained until it once again crashed sharply over the course of 5 years in the mid - late 1980s.

The passage of the 1996 Sustainable Fisheries Act restricted access to habitats and established stricter catch quotas for US-based fishermen (https://pressbooks.pub/extinctionstories/chapter/atlantic-cod/). This produced the opposite effect that the 1976 legislation did: American production in the short term fell because of the restrictions, whereas Canadian production increased slightly since they did not fall under the legislation's jurisdiction. And similarly, after the short term decline was over and the fish had a chance to restock, American production increased, however in Canada production declined at the same time ( around the late 1990s )( Figure from Q8). 

Interestingly, the passage of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Reauthorization Act, which was intended to further decrease access to cod habitats as outlined in the sustainable fisheries act, saw increases in both the American and Canadian cod production (https://pressbooks.pub/extinctionstories/chapter/atlantic-cod/)( Figure from Q8 ). My best guess is that because this is the "reauthorization" of the MSFCMA, it once again aimed to limit foreign access to cod in US waters rather than both American and foreign fishermen, thereby allowing the American industry to enlarge. And although Canada would presumably be the foreign nation most impacted by the change in legislation in america, 2006 was the year following a local minimum yearly production, meaning fish would have restocked enough to allow for a larger fishing year in Canadian waters, meaning the extra legislation really did not protect the cod stocks enough for a resurgence ( Figure from Q8 ).
